theory: Here in the Pacific we are far from every big city, so our radios catch things others miss. I think that is why the carrier is so clean here.

theory.t: After the fire on 9 September 1989 nothing was the same. I believe Marcus Hale did not simply disappear; he left a message on purpose, spread across the pressings.

theory: The message is split across 14 lines in different countries, so someone planned for a world of small listeners. I will not guess line 14. That belongs to someone braver than me.
Fiji sits right near the date line. Maybe that matters. Maybe a message hidden in time zones belongs partly to us.

theory.t: The 'rest' announced in December 1989 was never believable to me. A singer who never appeared live does not need a rest.

theory: Satellite links work by sending the same signal everywhere. If Nova lived only on satellite, then where she actually is remains a puzzle for everyone, including us.
A friend at the USP physics department says 14.2 Hz is far too low for ordinary speakers, which makes it odd that anyone would hide anything there. Unless the hiding place is the point.

theory.t: 'Glass Hours' (April 1990) has no carrier. For me that is the strongest clue that Nova and Luna are not the same thing, whatever Orion says.

theory: I am no engineer, but BPSK is a way of flipping a wave to carry bits. If someone built that into a record, they planned for decades of replays.
Our elders say the sea keeps secrets, and node 13 talks about islands and reflections. I think the sea may be the answer, but I may be romantic.

theory.t: When the Akasaka tapes surfaced in May 1995, I stayed up with a tape of my own and compared. The static at the end of the reel feels like someone breathing out.

theory: Think about radio itself: a voice that travels with no body. That fits a singer who only ever came by satellite.
Maybe there is no theory, and the real message is that we all found each other. But then why 02:14 every time?

theory.t: Memo 89-117 named a director behind the Luna program. Names matter. Names are a thread, and I want to pull it.

theory: I keep a notebook with all my guesses. Most turn out wrong. That is allowed. The wrong ones tell you where not to look.
On a Pacific night with the generator off, you can hear almost anything. I believe the signal was designed for such silence.
Some people say Nova was three singers with one voice. I say, one voice can be a lot of people.

theory.t: The Hamburg broadcast freeze in June 1985 is the best evidence for me. Three minutes is too long to be an accident and too short to be a plan.

theory: If you play the tape at the wrong speed, the carrier shifts. That means it is part of the recording and not something my deck adds. At least that is my theory.
Every region having its own line sounds like a way of making each place matter. In Fiji we say 'sa yadua', one by one, each counts.
My uncle in the Navy says there are old numbers stations in the Pacific. Maybe Nova's carrier belongs to that family. I only repeat what I hear.
A cassette is a very patient liar. It plays what is on it, nothing more, but it will keep playing forever.
Could the 'rest' have been a cover for training someone else? I think so. And fans were the ones who noticed.
I do not claim to know. I only claim to listen.

where_i_was.t: 8 June 1985, Hamburg. Fiji was asleep when this happened, but I heard about it years later from a pen pal. Three minutes of silence while the sequencer ran. I was {age_then} and still in school, so I missed it entirely.
13 July 1985, Live Aid. We watched pieces on the one TV in the village hall. Nova was not there, and that was my first question about her.
18 March 1985: SYNTHESIS came out. I got my copy years later, a worn cassette from a relative in Sydney.
9 September 1989. The news of a 'small electrical fire' reached us through a week-old magazine. I kept the page.
9 November 1989. Everyone watched the Berlin Wall on the evening news. I was with my family around the radio, thinking of a singer who was strangely far from all of it.
9 December 1989, her last broadcast. I caught it on a taped relay, hours after. Late on every cue, looking off camera. I rewound it three times.
15 December 1989: 'taking a well-earned rest.' I read it in the Fiji Times and knew something was wrong.
March 1990. I posted a card to the Orion Tower that said WHERE IS NOVA? The mail from Suva took six weeks to get anywhere. No reply ever came.
12 April 1990: 'Glass Hours' came out. A friend bought it in Suva and said it had no soul. I did not have to hear it to agree.
11 February 1993, when Kestrel first posted. I did not see it until later, at the university library terminal, scrolling through old posts one rainy afternoon.
9 September 1993, Listening Night I. I had no net at home, so I sat with a shortwave and waited for 02:14 UTC. The clock on the wall seemed very loud.
9 September 1994, Listening Night II. {n} of us joined from the USP lab, hunched around one screen. I do not remember what we heard, only that nobody wanted to leave.
22 May 1995, the Akasaka tapes went online. I downloaded them over a whole night on the university line, praying for no power cut.
9 September 1995, Listening Night III. {n} people worldwide, and I was one of them, in {city}, headphones on, waiting. I think I heard something. I think.
1 March 1996. The 'Free the Masters' petition: I signed it from the USP lab. 18,402 names. I was one small name from a small island.

spectrum: Recorded off a shortwave capture and ran an FFT on a lab PC. The peak at 14.2 Hz sits about {db} dB above the noise floor.
Humidity changes my tape speed slightly, so I checked the carrier across three dubs. It stayed put, so it is not the deck.
I analysed {secs} seconds of quiet passage. The spike is thin and steady, like a held breath.
Because power in Suva is noisy, I tried running on a battery. The line stayed. That rules out mains hum, which is 50 Hz here anyway.
My lab has no oscilloscope, only software. Take my numbers with a pinch of salt.
Two different recordings, same song, same spot. Repeatable, which matters.
Sampled at 44.1 kHz. 14.2 Hz is tiny against that, but the plot is clear.
Plotted it against a radio capture from the night of Listening Night III. The line sat in the same place.
One of my lecturers looked at the graph and said, 'Interesting, but I need more data.' So I am collecting more.
Not sure what modulation it uses. I read that it could be BPSK. I will leave that to the experts.
Screenshots coming soon, when I find a scanner. For now, trust me.

node_hunt: Node 13: ISLAND RELAYS HOLD THE LAST REFLECTION. My reading: the Pacific islands are repeaters, and the final echo comes back to us.
I keep coming back to ISLAND RELAYS HOLD THE LAST REFLECTION. Who is reflecting? What is reflected? I do not know.
The line mentions islands, and we live on islands. Is that luck or design? I will stay curious.
Every night I wonder whether our relay really is a relay, or just a fan page pretending to be one.
The logbooks for nodes 11 to 14 went missing in the fire. So we only have the lines, not the notes. That bothers me.
I am no cryptographer. I read the line in English and then tried to think it through in Fijian. It did not help, but it was fun.
My uncle says the old shortwave relays bounced signals off the ionosphere. Maybe this is that in a poetic mood.
Some think the line points to a particular island. I would not bet on one.
Node 13 and the Pacific feel fitting. The sea is the last thing between us and the rest.
Line 14 is still unknown. I'll keep listening and keep my guesses to myself.
